title: iPhone ProMotion 120Hz in Safari: Why Web Apps Run at 60Hz and How to Fix It
description: Comprehensive technical guide explaining why Apple WebKit throttles 120Hz ProMotion displays to 60Hz in mobile Safari, the CADisplayLink rendering pipeline, and how to unlock full 120Hz web animation.
author: ToolkitGen Engineering Team
quickAnswer: Apple WebKit intentionally throttles requestAnimationFrame to 60Hz in Safari on iOS, even on 120Hz ProMotion displays (iPhone 13 Pro through 16 Pro and iPad Pro). This limit is enforced by an internal battery-conservation feature flag: 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps'. You can unlock full 120Hz rendering in Safari by navigating to iOS Settings > Apps > Safari > Advanced > Feature Flags, turning off 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps', and restarting Safari.
articleHtml:
The ProMotion 120Hz Paradox: Native Fluidity vs WebKit Throttling

When Apple debuted ProMotion variable refresh technology on the iPhone 13 Pro in 2021, users experienced ultra-smooth 120Hz scrolling across iOS system menus and native App Store applications. However, web developers, mobile gamers, and technology enthusiasts immediately identified an unexpected bottleneck: web animations, interactive canvas games, and requestAnimationFrame loops in Safari remained firmly capped at 60 frames per second.

ProMotion Frame Rate Allocation Comparison

Native iOS Cocoa Touch Apps

10Hz to 120Hz Dynamic Range. Powered by CADisplayLink and UIKit springs. Dynamically scales down to 10Hz for static reading and scales up to 120Hz during active touch dragging.

Default Mobile Safari (iOS)

60Hz Hard Throttle. Apple WebKit locks requestAnimationFrame to ~16.67 ms ticks to protect battery life under the 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps' policy.

Unlocked Safari ProMotion

120Hz High-Refresh Pacing. Disabling the feature flag in Safari Advanced Settings releases rAF callbacks to full 8.33 ms frame delivery.

1. The Underpinnings: How CADisplayLink Powers ProMotion

To comprehend why mobile Safari restricts web animations, one must examine how iOS coordinates screen refreshes at the operating system kernel level.

On iOS, display updates are orchestrated by the Core Animation framework through a specialized timer class called CADisplayLink. In traditional 60Hz displays, the display controller emits a vertical blanking interrupt (V-Sync) at a fixed cadence every 16.667 milliseconds:

$$\Delta t_{60\text{Hz}} = \frac{1000\text{ ms}}{60} \approx 16.667\text{ ms}$$

With ProMotion, Apple transitioned to Low-Temperature Polycrystalline Oxide (LTPO) OLED panels capable of dynamic refresh modulation. ProMotion panels do not run continuously at 120Hz; doing so would increase display subsystem power draw by up to 40%. Instead, the display controller dynamically shifts between discrete refresh targets:

  • 10 Hz (100.0 ms hold): Static text reading or Always-On Display.
  • 24 Hz / 30 Hz (41.67 ms / 33.33 ms): Video playback matching cinematic frame rates.
  • 60 Hz (16.67 ms): Standard UI motion or low-power state.
  • 80 Hz / 120 Hz (12.5 ms / 8.33 ms): High-speed thumb flicks, game rendering, and rapid momentum panning.

In native Swift/Objective-C applications, developers define frame rate preferences using preferredFrameRateRange, declaring minimum, preferred, and maximum boundaries. The iOS compositor prioritizes the user's physical finger velocity: as soon as a touch contact begins, the display instantly jumps to 120Hz.

2. Why WebKit Defaults to 60fps: The Battery Conservation Mandate

Unlike native applications curated through the strict App Store review process, web applications execute arbitrary third-party JavaScript code. On the open web, thousands of websites deploy continuous requestAnimationFrame loops for non-critical visual decorations—such as floating background particles, ticker marquees, or continuous parallax calculations.

If Safari ran all requestAnimationFrame callbacks at 120Hz unconditionally, the GPU and mobile CPU would execute twice as many layout recalibrations, style evaluations, and composite passes. On mobile devices with constrained thermal envelopes and 3,200 to 4,400 mAh batteries, unthrottled 120Hz web rendering would result in rapid battery drain and aggressive thermal throttling.

Consequently, Apple WebKit engineers instituted a defensive architectural policy [Confirmed: WebKit Bugzilla]:

  1. Native Browser Chrome & Page Scrolling: The native Safari address bar, tab switcher, and kinetic momentum scrolling of the root web document operate at 120Hz because they are managed directly by Core Animation in the iOS compositor.
  2. JavaScript DOM & Canvas Rendering: Internal web page animations driven by JavaScript requestAnimationFrame are capped at 60Hz via the internal feature flag Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps.

3. Step-by-Step Instructions: How to Unlock 120Hz ProMotion in Safari

For power users, mobile gamers playing web-based titles, and developers benchmarking WebGL or WebGPU applications, Apple provides a native mechanism to disable this throttle.

  1. Open iOS Settings: Tap the Settings icon on your iPhone or iPad home screen.
  2. Locate Safari Preferences:
    • On iOS 18+: Scroll down and tap Apps, then scroll to Safari.
    • On iOS 17 and earlier: Scroll directly down the main Settings menu to Safari.
  3. Navigate to Advanced Features: Scroll to the very bottom of the Safari menu and tap Advanced.
  4. Open Feature Flags: Tap Feature Flags (labeled Experimental Features on older iOS versions).
  5. Toggle 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps': Scroll through the alphabetical list to find Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps. Toggle the switch to OFF.
  6. Force Restart Safari: Swipe up from the bottom of your screen to enter the App Switcher, swipe up on Safari to force close the process, and reopen the browser.

Once completed, open our iPhone & Mobile Browser Capability Checker. The live delivered refresh rate counter will now display a fluid 120Hz with frame deltas averaging 8.33 milliseconds.

4. Best Practices for High-Framerate Mobile Web Development

Web developers designing interactive experiences for ProMotion displays should adopt defensive coding patterns:

  • Never Assume 60Hz Delta Math: Avoid hardcoding 16.67ms or 1/60 into physics simulation loops. Always compute elapsed time dynamically via the high-resolution timestamp passed to the requestAnimationFrame(now) callback:
    function animate(now) {
      const dt = (now - lastTime) / 1000; // in seconds
      lastTime = now;
      position += velocity * dt;
      requestAnimationFrame(animate);
    }
  • Harness CSS Transforms & Will-Change: Use transform: translate3d(x, y, 0) and will-change: transform to promote moving layers to dedicated GPU backing stores, bypassing CPU rasterization bottlenecks.
  • Halt Inactive Loops: Use the Page Visibility API (document.hidden) to suspend animation loops when the tab is backgrounded or hidden.

faq.q: Does unlocking 120Hz in Safari significantly reduce battery life?
faq.a: On well-coded web pages that only animate during user interaction, the impact on battery life is minimal (typically under 5%). However, if you keep tabs open that run heavy continuous 3D canvas animations or particle loops, power consumption can increase by 20% to 30%.

faq.q: Do Chrome and Firefox for iOS support 120Hz ProMotion?
faq.a: Because Apple App Store guidelines mandate that all third-party browsers on iOS use the WebKit engine, Chrome and Firefox for iOS inherit WebKit's default 60Hz requestAnimationFrame behavior.

faq.q: Why does my iPhone 13 Pro drop back to 60Hz when Low Power Mode is on?
faq.a: Low Power Mode forces the iOS compositor to cap maximum display refresh at 60Hz system-wide, disabling ProMotion 120Hz across all native applications and web browsers to conserve power.

faq.q: How can I verify if my device actually has a ProMotion 120Hz screen?
faq.a: ProMotion is exclusive to Pro models: iPhone 13 Pro / Pro Max, iPhone 14 Pro / Pro Max, iPhone 15 Pro / Pro Max, iPhone 16 Pro / Pro Max, and iPad Pro models since 2017. Standard non-Pro iPhones (e.g. iPhone 13, 14, 15, 16) feature fixed 60Hz panels.
